paragraphs: Naturally Favorable to the Concentration of Power

Aristocratic nations came naturally to imagine secondary powers standing between the sovereign and his subjects. Their communities held individuals or families set above the common level, who seemed destined to command through birth, education and wealth. Men in democratic ages lack this idea naturally, for the opposite reasons. It can be brought in only artificially and kept only with effort. What they do grasp, almost without reflecting on it, is the idea of one central power governing the whole community by direct influence. In politics, as in philosophy and religion, the intellect of democratic nations is also especially receptive to simple, general ideas. Complicated systems repel it. Its favorite picture is a great nation of citizens who all fit the same pattern and are all governed by a single power.

Next to the idea of one central power, the notion that occurs most readily to men in ages of equality is uniform legislation. Each man sees that he is not very different from those around him. He cannot see why a rule that suits one person should not suit everyone else. Even the slightest privilege therefore offends his reason, and the faintest variation in a single people’s political institutions irritates him. To him, uniform legislation is the first condition of good government. In aristocratic ages, I find, the human mind knew almost nothing of a uniform rule binding equally on every member of the community; people either never thought of it or rejected it. On each side, these opposing tendencies of opinion end up as blind instincts and uncontrollable habits, so that they still guide men’s actions despite individual exceptions. The Middle Ages had an immense variety of conditions, and a certain number of people were then in exactly similar circumstances. Even so, the laws of the time gave each of them different duties and different rights. Today, by contrast, every power of government is being used to impose the same customs and laws on populations that so far have few points in common. When the conditions of men become equal within a people, individuals appear less important and society looms larger. Or, more exactly, each citizen is made like all the others and gets lost in the crowd, and nothing stands out except the great and imposing image of the people as a whole. The men of democratic periods are naturally led to think very highly of society’s privileges and very modestly of individuals’ rights. They are ready to grant that the interests of the first are everything and those of the second nothing. They will accept that the power representing the community has much more information and wisdom than any of its members, and that it has both the duty and the right to guide each private citizen as well as to govern him.

Look closely at our contemporaries and dig down to the roots of their political opinions, and you will meet some of the ideas I have just described. The agreement may perhaps come as a surprise, among men who so often disagree. Americans hold that in every State the supreme power ought to come from the people. Once that power exists, however, they can imagine hardly any limit to it, and they are ready to concede that it has the right to do whatever it likes. They have not the faintest notion of special privileges for cities, families or persons. It seems never to have occurred to them that the same laws might fail to be applied, with strict uniformity, to every part and every inhabitant. These same opinions are spreading further in Europe. They are even working their way into the nations that most vehemently reject the sovereignty of the people. Those nations trace the supreme power to a different source but attribute the same characteristics to it. In all of them the idea of intermediate powers is growing faint and being erased. The idea of rights belonging inherently to certain individuals is fast vanishing from men’s minds, and the idea that society at large is omnipotent and sole authority is rising to fill the space. As social conditions grow more equal and men more alike, these ideas take root and spread. Equality produces them, and they in turn speed equality along.

In France, the revolution I am discussing has gone further than anywhere else in Europe, and these opinions there have taken full possession of the public mind. Listen carefully to what the various French parties say, and you will find that every one has adopted them. Most of the parties condemn the government’s conduct, but all of them believe it should act without pause and meddle in everything that is done. Even the parties most opposed to each other agree on this. The unity, ubiquity and omnipotence of the supreme power, together with the uniformity of its rules, are the principal characteristics of all the political systems put forward in our age. They turn up even in the wildest visions of political regeneration, and the human mind chases them in its dreams. If private individuals come to these ideas spontaneously, princes feel their pull still more strongly. The ancient fabric of European society is being altered and dissolved. Sovereigns are forming new conceptions of what they can do and what they owe. They are learning, for the first time, that the central power they stand for may and should administer all the affairs of the whole community through its own agents, on a single plan. I will venture to say that no monarch in Europe had conceived this opinion before our time. It now sinks deep into the minds of kings and remains there amid every stirring of more restless thought.

Our contemporaries are therefore far less divided than people usually suppose. They argue endlessly about whose hands should hold supremacy, yet they readily agree about what that supremacy should do and what rights it has. All of them picture government as a single, simple, providential and creative power. Every other political opinion is unsettled, but this one stays fixed, unvarying and consistent. Statesmen and political philosophers embrace it, and the multitude seizes on it eagerly. Rulers and ruled alike pursue it with equal ardor. It is the first idea in their minds, and it seems inborn. It does not, then, spring from any whim of the human intellect. It is a necessary condition of mankind’s present state.
